Jawbone
JAW-bone
noun
From jaw, of uncertain Northern origin, with bone; rendering the Hebrew lechi, the jaw or cheek, which also gave its name to the place Lehi where Samson fought, and to Ramath-lehi, the lifting up of the jawbone.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The jawbone enters Scripture as the least likely weapon ever carried into a battle. Bound with new cords and delivered to the Philistines at Lehi, Samson felt the Spirit of the LORD come mightily upon him, and the cords became as burnt flax (Jdg 15:14); then “he found a new jawbone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith” (Jdg 15:15). Every particular of the instrument is a disqualification. It is bone, not iron, in an age when Israel had no smith; it is the jaw of an ass, the unclean beast of burden; and it is found lying on the ground, neither forged nor bought nor chosen. Against it stood a nation with chariots. The point is not Samson’s strength, which was never his own — the text says plainly that the Spirit of the LORD came upon him first — but God’s settled way of working. He saves by ram’s horns and clay pitchers, by a sling and a stone, by five loaves, by the foolishness of preaching: “God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27). Samson afterward named the place Ramath-lehi and, dying of thirst in his victory, called on the LORD and was given water — lest the man who had just killed a thousand should imagine the arm was his. The jawbone is a sermon on means: God’s power is glorified in instruments that can claim nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

The bone of the jaw, in which the teeth are fixed; famously the weapon Samson found at Lehi and with which he slew a thousand Philistines.

expand to see more

JAWBONE, n. The bone of either jaw, in which the teeth are fixed.

From jaw and bone; the Hebrew word lechi denotes the jaw or the cheek.

The same word names the place Lehi, and Ramath-lehi, the lifting up of the jawbone (Jdg 15:17).

The weapon with which Samson slew a thousand men (Jdg 15:15–16).

Hence proverbially, an instrument of no account made mighty by the hand that wields it.

Key Scripture

Jdg 15:14 — "And when he came unto Lehi, the Philistines shouted against him: and the Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him, and the cords that were upon his arms became as flax that was burnt with fire, and his bands loosed from off his hands."

Jdg 15:15 — "And he found a new jawbone of an ass, and put forth his hand, and took it, and slew a thousand men therewith."

1Co 1:27 — "But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty;"

2Co 12:9 — "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Modern Corruption

The common misuse turns Samson into a strongman and the jawbone into a trophy of personal grit, when the text puts the Spirit of the LORD before the weapon and thirst after the victory.

expand to see more

The live misuse is heroic moralism. Samson is preached as a study in wasted potential or, worse, as an emblem of raw masculine force, and the jawbone becomes a symbol of what a determined man can do with whatever is at hand — a proverb for self-reliance. The narrative resists that reading at every turn. The Spirit of the LORD came mightily upon him before he touched the bone (Jdg 15:14); the weapon was found, not made; the man who had slain a thousand collapsed within the hour, so athirst that he thought he would die and fall into the hand of the uncircumcised, and had to beg water of the God he had just been used by. Samson is not the point of Samson. He is a judge raised, gifted, indulged, and finally broken, whose deliverances are God’s and whose sins are his own, and the Spirit-given strength never once became a possession he could manage. Read as self-help, the chapter flatters the reader; read as it stands, it humbles him.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God chooses unlikely means so that the glory cannot be reassigned. “God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty” (1Co 1:27), and Paul learned the same lesson in his own flesh: strength made perfect in weakness (2Co 12:9). The pattern runs the length of Scripture — a shepherd’s sling against a giant, trumpets against a walled city, a boy’s loaves against a hungry multitude, and at the centre a crucified Man against the powers of darkness, which is the greatest apparent weakness and the actual conquest. The comfort for the ordinary believer is direct: God is not waiting for you to become a suitable instrument. The jawbone of an ass was not upgraded before it was used. What He requires is a hand that will pick it up when He says so, and a mouth that will ask Him for water afterward instead of composing a song about its own arm.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The bone of the jaw; the found, unclean, unlikely weapon by which God delivered Israel through Samson at Lehi.

expand to see more

Jawbone — jaw + bone; Hebrew lechi, jaw or cheek.

Lehi the place and lechi the jaw are the same word (Jdg 15:9, 15).

Ramath-lehi = the lifting up (or casting away) of the jawbone (Jdg 15:17).

The bone of an ass is unclean, brittle, and found — every disqualification at once.

The Spirit precedes the weapon in the text; the order is the doctrine.

Usage

"Jdg 15:14 comes before Jdg 15:15: the Spirit first, the jawbone second."

"God’s instruments are chosen for their unfitness, that no flesh should glory."

"Samson begging water an hour after slaying a thousand is the safeguard against hero-worship."
